extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP lawyers, patent examiners, and policymakers concerned with Canadian patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes and explains Canadian statutory and practice-oriented standards for: grace periods/non‑prejudicial disclosures, prior user rights (Section 56), and treatment of conflicting applications/secret prior art, including anti‑double‑patenting principles and related procedural points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period: duration and basic scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration: 12 months. Calculated from: Filing date in Canada. Covers all types of disclosures by, for or derived from the inventor or their successor in title, regardless of medium or forum, and regardless of whether intentional or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace period may be invoked throughout the life of the patent. Applicant must be identified as the source when applicable (see statement/declaration and burden of proof references). Publication of the application for which the grace period has been invoked is relevant to invoking the grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period does not cover disclosures resulting from patent office publication at 18 months
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures resulting from the proper publication of an application by an office at 18 months are not graced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant cannot rely on the domestic grace period to neutralize the effect of that office publication as prior art; publication at 18 months stands as prior art for later applications unless other statutory exceptions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's own previously published application may be graced
rubrics_metrics.description: The grace period in Canada applies to an applicant’s own previously published application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication of the applicant's own prior application can be treated as a non‑prejudicial disclosure within the grace period, subject to the statutory and evidentiary requirements (see statements/declarations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party independent disclosures not graced (secret prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures of independent inventions made by a third party form part of the prior art (i.e., are not graced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent third‑party activity is treated as prior art against later applications; such disclosures do not benefit from the inventor's grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: No on‑sale bar in Canada
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no on‑sale bar in Canada (the concept of an on‑sale bar is not part of Canadian law as presented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Industry Trilateral 2021 'Elements' paper may discuss on‑sale bar concepts, but they are not operative as a bar under Canadian practice outlined here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence of Intervening User (DIU)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defence of Intervening User is listed as a relevant concept alongside grace period/on‑sale considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No detailed statutory text provided on the page; shows DIU is a recognized defense concept to be considered in Canadian practice discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user rights (PURs) statutory basis and threshold acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory basis: Section 56 of the Patent Act. Conditions for PURs to arise: commercial use or serious and effective preparations to use that would otherwise constitute infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A qualified prior user must have performed acts that would be infringing or made serious and effective preparations. Critical date: qualifying activities must take place prior to the earliest of the filing or priority date. References to sections 56 and 28.1 appear relevant to timing and claim date considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: PURs: relation to derived non‑public information
rubrics_metrics.description: PURs when use based on non‑public information derived from the applicant without his consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes situations where the third party's use is based on information derived from the applicant (e.g., through a pre‑filing disclosure). Subsection 56(5) is referenced with respect to knowledge of source; the distinction between independent invention and derived knowledge affects entitlement to PURs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good faith and derivation standards for PURs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use based on independent invention by the third party gives rise to rights; prior user rights if the third party has derived his knowledge of the invention from the applicant (e.g., through a PFD) are treated specially; good faith requirement for PURs to accrue is considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document records nuanced lines: independent invention can give PURs; derivation from applicant may affect entitlement depending on knowledge/source; courts will analyze facts of derivation and good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for claiming PURs
rubrics_metrics.description: Burden of proof that prior activities justify a PUR rests on the prior user claiming the PUR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimant must show on the relevant dates that the necessary commercial use or preparations existed and meet statutory requirements; the PUR defense is assessed claim‑by‑claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of PURs (claim‑by‑claim and changes permitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: PUR applies on a claim‑by‑claim basis. Prior user may make changes so long as they do not relate to the inventive concept of the patent (see Kobold Corporation et al v NCS Multistage Inc, 2021 FC 1437).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will permit evolution of the prior user's embodiment provided changes do not encroach on the inventive concept protected by the patent; scope is therefore limited to what the prior use effectively covered per claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer and licensing of PURs
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer of PURs is permitted only if transferred together with the related business within which it accrued. Licensing under the PUR: see subsection 56(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PURs are personal to the business/use and generally cannot be severed from the business unless statutory or case law permits; subsection 56(2) provides further authority on licensing—consult the Act for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial scope of PRIOR USER RIGHTS
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial scope of PURs limited to the country in which the prior use/preparations took place (Patent Act only applies in Canada).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Canadian PUR protects prior use within Canada only; it does not automatically create rights in other jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting applications: whole‑contents approach for secret prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing earlier applications that are secret prior art, the whole contents approach applies: the entire contents of the earlier application form secret prior art for the later filed application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with a 'prior claiming' approach where only subject matter that was claimed in the prior application would count. Jurisdictional differences may affect whether whole‑contents or prior‑claiming approach is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret prior art: later application must be novel over whole earlier application
rubrics_metrics.description: The later filed application must be novel over the whole contents of the earlier filed application that is secret prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The earlier application's full disclosure can be used to destroy novelty of claims in the later application even if the earlier application was not publicly available at the time (i.e., treated as secret prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑double‑patenting and purposive construction for obviousness‑type double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Same applicant: No two patents shall issue with claims to the same invention or claims that are not patentably distinct. For obviousness‑type double patenting, claims are given a purposive construction based on reading the specification through the eyes of the skilled person, taking into account common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claims of the existing patent, as understood by the person skilled in the art in light of CGK on the claim date and the teachings of the specification as a whole, anticipate or render obvious the claims of the application being examined, the claims are not patentably distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT and co‑pending national applications as conflicting applications / secret prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: PCT applications should form conflicting applications and become secret prior art upon national entry into Canada. They are treated similarly to other co‑pending applications with respect to dates of publication and conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon national entry into Canada the PCT application becomes part of the secret prior art picture; the date of publication of the application is relevant for co‑pending application treatment.
